title: Multi-armed bandits: post-test
note: The final test is form A, the same for everyone (`final`, 2026-11-12): seven items in a fixed order, from greedy to the price of exploring: T1 (greedy after a lucky start), T12 (lock-in from a small dip), V14 (which episodes UCB could recommend, in T4's place: stronger wrong options), V7 (UCB shows the worse banner more when the two are close; a placeholder), V4 (UCB keeps returning to the worst option, with ever longer gaps), T6 (a bonus that stops growing), V19 (the price of exploring, rewritten without c). Form B holds the pilot's candidates, asked after the final test only with both forms (the pilot code): V1 (an optimistic start), V15 (T12's twin, to compare), T7 (two equally good options: V7's idea from another side) and V21 (four logs to match to the rules). T16 (too easy), T4 and V20 (on c, which leaves the lesson) are in stash/exercises.json with every other item.

items.title: Canteens
items.prompt: A team picks one of three canteens each day with greedy and scores each lunch out of 10. The true averages, unknown to the team, are A 7, B 6 and C 4; most lunches score within 1 point of them. On the three trial days A scores 6.5, B has an exceptionally good lunch and scores 9, and C scores 4. In the long run, over many years, where does the team eat on most days?
options: At B
At A
At A and B, about equally often
It depends on whether B has more exceptional lunches
items.explain: Greedy first picks B, which has the highest average. B keeps being tried, and its lunches of about 5 to 7 pull its average towards 6. After about 7 lunches it falls below A's 6.5, and greedy switches to A. A's average settles near 7, above B's, which no longer changes.
items.rubric: B keeps being tried, so its too-high average falls below A's; A then stays ahead.
diagnosis: Kai: F4 (greedy commits after the first tries)
correct
learner: greedy alternates when averages are close
learner: the outcome is down to luck
items.note: In 2,000 simulated years greedy ate at A on 97% of days. 2026-11-05: "in the long run, over many years" instead of "the following year": a pilot learner saw B's average sink but wasn't sure a year was long enough.

items.title: Study spots
items.prompt: A student picks one of two study spots each evening with greedy and rates each evening's focus out of 10. Spot A is truly better: its evenings usually score between 7 and 9. Spot B's evenings always score between 6 and 7. On the two trial evenings, A scores 5.5, a bit below its usual, and B scores 6.5. What does greedy do for the rest of the term?
options: It switches between A and B for a while, since their averages are close
It goes back to A once B's average drops a little
It never picks A again, all term
It goes back to A after a while, once A's average has corrected itself
items.explain: After the trials B leads, 6.5 to 5.5, so greedy picks B. Every evening at B scores at least 6, so B's average never drops below 6, which stays above A's 5.5. A is never picked again, so its 5.5 is never corrected: a first try only a little below its usual is enough to lock greedy out of the better spot.
items.rubric: B's average can't fall below A's 5.5 (B never scores below 6); A isn't picked again, so its average is never corrected.
diagnosis: learner: greedy alternates when averages are close
learner: overlooks that B never scores below 6, so B's average can't fall below 5.5
correct
Kai: F5 (averages correct themselves, so greedy finds the best in the end)
items.note: New 2026-11-05 (ε-greedy left the lesson), in t03's place. Lock-in from a small dip rather than a disaster, with a bound to check: a step past Kai's lock-in question, easier than t01 (a too-high start that corrects itself). The key follows from the bounds; no simulation needed. "Never picks A again" can also come from Kai's F4 belief (greedy commits after the first tries): the reason tells them apart.

items.title: Episodes
items.prompt: A podcast app recommends one of four episodes with UCB. All of the following is for the same round. Episode A averages 4.6 (200 times), B 4.1 (15 times), C 4.6 (90 times) and D 3.5 (15 times). Which episodes could UCB recommend next? (Tip: you don't need to calculate to solve this exercise.)
options: A or C
B or D
Any of the four
B or C
items.explain: UCB picks the highest average plus bonus, and within one round fewer tries means a larger bonus. C beats A: the same average, fewer tries. B beats D: the same tries, a higher average. C against B depends on the sizes of the bonuses, which are not given.
items.rubric: Rules out A and D by these comparisons; B against C cannot be decided.
diagnosis: learner: the best average wins, as with greedy (ties broken by the averages alone)
Kai: F9 (picks the fewest tries)
learner: without the bonus values any option could win
correct
items.note: The twin of T4 (2026-11-05). 2026-11-12 (Phil): in the final test in T4's place, whose wrong options were weaker; the sentence on the bonus formula not being given replaced by a tip.

items.title: Close or far apart
items.prompt: Two shops use UCB with two banners each for 10,000 visitors. In shop 1 the banners' true click rates are 90% and 10%; in shop 2 they are 51% and 49%. In which shop does UCB show the worse banner more often?
options: About equally often in both shops
In shop 2
In shop 1
In neither shop, after the first few visitors
items.explain: UCB shows the worse banner whenever its average plus bonus beats the better banner's score. The worse banner's bonus shrinks with each show in the same way in both shops. In shop 1 the averages are 80 points apart, so the worse banner loses once its bonus falls below that, after few shows; in shop 2 they are 2 points apart, so it keeps winning until its bonus is tiny, which takes thousands of shows.
items.rubric: Whether the bonus wins depends on the gap between averages; a small gap is overcome only by a tiny bonus, which needs many shows.
diagnosis: learner: the bonus doesn't depend on the rewards, so the gap between the banners doesn't matter
correct
learner: a very bad option needs more checking
Kai: F11 (an unpicked bonus stays the same)
items.note: In simulation (50 runs) UCB showed the worse banner 26 times in shop 1 and 3,553 times in shop 2. 2026-11-12: in the final test as a placeholder (it may be easy; T7 tests the same idea from another side in the pilot).

items.title: Forever
items.prompt: UCB runs forever on four options. Option D is clearly the worst, and by round 10,000 UCB's averages show this. How does UCB treat D from then on?
options: D is picked again only if its average rises
After some round, D is no longer picked
D keeps being picked, with ever longer gaps
D is picked at a roughly fixed share of rounds
items.explain: While D is not picked, its bonus keeps growing with the round number, without limit. So D's score eventually beats the best option's, and D is picked again. Each pick shrinks D's bonus, and the regrowth gets ever slower, so each gap is longer than the last.
items.rubric: The bonus of an unpicked option grows without limit; each pick shrinks it, and regrowth slows.
diagnosis: learner: UCB treated like greedy
Kai: F11 (an unpicked bonus stays the same), or F10 (every bonus shrinks over time)
correct
Kai: F11 vague (the bonus grows at a steady rate)
items.note: The twin of T6 (2026-11-05): both ask how an option the averages show to be worse fares from then on, T6 under a changed bonus, V4 under ordinary UCB.

items.title: A bonus that stops growing
items.prompt: A developer changes UCB: the bonus still shrinks each time an option is tried, but it no longer grows with the round number. Option A is truly better (average 8), but its 5 tries were unusually low, and its score (average plus bonus) is now 5.5. Option B has been tried 40 times and always scores between 6 and 7. What does the changed UCB do from now on?
options: It picks A in the next round
It picks A again after a while
It picks A again once B's bonus has shrunk enough
It never picks A again
items.explain: UCB picks the higher score, now B's, which is at least B's average, so at least 6. A is not picked, so its average and its tries stay the same, and in this version its bonus does not grow either: A's score stays at 5.5. B's score never falls below 6, so A is never picked again, the same lock-in as with greedy.
items.rubric: A's score is frozen; B's score stays above it.
diagnosis: Kai: F9 (picks the fewest tries)
learner: answers for ordinary UCB and ignores the change
learner: overlooks that B's average alone beats 5.5
correct

items.title: The price of exploring
items.prompt: Two vending machines each choose which of three snacks to put in the front slot every day: one uses greedy, the other UCB. A snack's daily sales score always lands within 2 points of its true average, which the machines don't know: A 7, B 6 and C 3. On the three trial days both machines happen to get the same scores: A 9, B 4 and C 1. In the long run, which machine can expect the higher total score?
options: The greedy machine
The UCB machine
About the same for both
It depends on A's next few scores
items.explain: After the trials, greedy's favourite is A, which is truly the best. A's scores never fall below 5, so its average stays above B's 4 and C's 1, and greedy picks A every day: B's and C's averages are never corrected, but here that costs nothing. UCB keeps coming back to B and C now and then, because their bonuses keep growing while they aren't picked, and each of those days scores lower on average than A would. So greedy collects more: exploring has a price when the first favourite happens to be the right one.
items.rubric: Greedy stays on A, which is truly the best (A's average can't fall below 5, above B's 4); UCB keeps spending some days on B and C (their bonuses keep growing), and those cost score.
diagnosis: correct
learner: exploring always pays, so UCB always does better than greedy
Kai: F11 (an unpicked bonus stays the same, so UCB soon stops trying B and C) or learner: exploring costs nothing once the best is found
learner: overlooks that A's average can't fall below 5, above B's 4, so greedy never leaves A
items.note: Rewritten 2026-11-12 (Phil): the same mechanism without the setting c (which leaves the lesson) and without the podcasts and listens (V14 has podcasts): vending machines, in the long run. The key follows from the lesson's rules: greedy never leaves A (A's scores of at least 5 keep its average above B's 4), and UCB must come back to B and C again and again, since an unpicked bonus grows without limit, and each of those days costs. Before (podcasts, 1,000 listens, c fitted to ratings 0 to 10, 200 simulated runs): UCB behind greedy in 189 of 200; in the long run UCB's extra picks of B and C keep growing (like ln t) while greedy's cost stays zero.

items.title: Optimistic start
items.prompt: A developer changes greedy: before the first round, every option's average is set to 10, the top score, as if each had already been tried once and scored 10. The three options truly average 7, 6 and 4, and daily scores vary by up to 3 points either way. Compared with ordinary greedy, how often does it end up mostly on the best option?
options: About as often
More often
Less often
items.explain: Whichever option is picked first gets a real score below 10, so its average falls below the others' 10. Greedy then picks an option still at 10, so every option gets tried, and too-high averages keep being tried until they fall. No option starts too low, which is what causes lock-in, so it ends up on the best option more often.
items.rubric: Averages start too high, so each option keeps being tried until its average falls; nothing starts too low, so lock-in is rarer.
diagnosis: Kai: F5 (averages correct themselves, so the start does not matter)
correct
learner: the made-up starting values mislead it
items.note: In 3,000 simulated runs ordinary greedy ended mostly at the best option in 79% of runs, optimistic greedy in 99% (Sutton & Barto, §2.6). Revised after the pretest review; three options suffice here.

items.title: Coffee shops
items.prompt: A commuter picks one of two coffee shops each morning with greedy and rates each coffee out of 10. Shop A is truly better: its coffees usually score between 8 and 9. Shop B's coffees always score between 6.5 and 7.5. On the two trial mornings, A scores 6, a bit below its usual, and B scores 7. What does greedy do for the rest of the year?
options: It never picks A again, all year
It switches between A and B for a while, since their averages are close
It goes back to A once B's average drops a little
It goes back to A after a while, once A's average has corrected itself
items.explain: After the trials B leads, 7 to 6, so greedy picks B. Every morning at B scores at least 6.5, so B's average never drops below 6.5, which stays above A's 6. A is never picked again, so its 6 is never corrected: a first try only a little below its usual is enough to lock greedy out of the better shop.
items.rubric: B's average can't fall below A's 6 (B never scores below 6.5); A isn't picked again, so its average is never corrected.
diagnosis: correct
learner: greedy alternates when averages are close
learner: overlooks that B never scores below 6.5, so B's average can't fall below 6
Kai: F5 (averages correct themselves, so greedy finds the best in the end)
items.note: The twin of T12 (Phil's lock-in from a small dip, 2026-11-05) in another setting. 2026-11-12: back from the stash as a pilot candidate, to compare with T12.

items.title: Two equally good options
items.prompt: UCB runs on three options. A and B are truly equally good; C is clearly worse. After the first 1,000 rounds, A has been picked 600 times, B 300 times and C 100 times, so B has one third of the picks that went to A or B. What happens to B's share over the next 100,000 rounds?
options: It falls towards zero
It rises towards one half
It stays at about one third
It rises, and C also catches up with A and B
items.explain: A's and B's averages both approach the same true average. B has fewer tries, so a larger bonus. With nearly equal averages the larger bonus decides, so UCB picks B more often than A until their counts are close. C's lower average keeps it rare.
items.rubric: The option with fewer tries has the larger bonus; with equal averages that decides.
diagnosis: learner: the leader takes over, as with greedy
correct
learner: UCB keeps the proportions it has reached
Kai: F9 (picks the fewest tries)
items.note: In 40 simulated runs, B's share rose from one third to between 0.38 and 0.76 (median 0.50). Adapted from midterm Q11. 2026-11-12: back from the stash as a pilot candidate: V7's idea (with close averages the bonus decides) from another side; could replace V7.

items.title: Four logs
items.prompt: Four logs count how often the worst of four options was picked in three periods, one run each. Each period is ten times as long as the one before. One log comes from greedy and one from UCB; the other two come from programs that follow neither rule.
items.question: Which log comes from greedy, and which from UCB?
options: Greedy W, UCB Y
Greedy Y, UCB X
Greedy W, UCB X
Greedy W, UCB Z
items.explain: W is greedy: once the worst option's average is behind after its one trial, greedy never picks it again, since it only ever takes the favourite (W: the trial pick, then none). X is UCB: each pick shrinks the worst option's bonus, and while it isn't picked the bonus grows back, ever more slowly, so UCB keeps coming back with ever longer gaps (about the same number of picks in each period, although each is ten times as long). Y picks it at the same share of every period (5%), which neither rule does; Z stops picking it, which UCB doesn't, since an unpicked bonus grows without limit.
items.rubric: Greedy stops after the trial (it never picks an option to learn about it); UCB keeps returning with ever longer gaps (about the same number of picks in each tenfold-longer period: the bonus grows back ever more slowly).
diagnosis: Kai: F11 vague (the bonus grows at a steady rate, so a neglected option comes back at regular intervals)
learner: greedy keeps trying other options now and then
correct
Kai: F11 (an unpicked bonus stays the same, so UCB stops picking the worst option), or F10 (every bonus shrinks over time)
items.note: New 2026-11-12 (Phil's idea): match logs of picks of the worst option to the rules, with two logs that fit neither, so no option looks unlikely. X is t14's simulation (four options with true averages 0.7, 0.6, 0.5 and 0.3, rewards spread around them with sd 0.25 and kept between 0 and 1, UCB with c = √2, means of 20 runs: 5.2%, 0.61% and 0.05% of the periods, about 50 picks each, since picks grow like ln t); greedy picked the worst option only on its trial in 88% of 200 runs. Y (a fixed 5%) and Z (stopping) are made up: neither rule produces them. V4's idea (UCB's ever longer gaps) and greedy's lock-in, read from data: could replace V4 or V7.
